speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the importance of the question asked by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands. I read the story in the Montreal Gazette this morning; obviously, as the hon. member knows, the story is inaccurate. If I may respond directly to the hon. member's question, there has been no further documentation or proposal made since the Prime Minister tabled copies of his letters to the premiers respecting the patriation exercise of April 10, 1976, to which a draft proclamation was appended. This draft proclamation is falsely drawn upon to support the allegation that the draft proclamation itself removes existing guarantees with respect to language rights.
I think Article 30 of the draft proclamation is explicit and states that English and French are the official languages of Canada, that no provision in this part shall derogate from any right, privilege or obligation existing under any other provision of the constitution.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Mr. Speaker, I will try as briefly as I can to answer what is a very complex question. There were very detailed discussions between myself and the United States Secretary on this matter. Prior to my going to Washington there were also talks between officials and there have been follow-up talks which were held yesterday. They covered most of the questions the hon. member has raised in a general discussion fashion. As things stand at the moment, the Secretary and I have agreed that it would not be possible in the period between now and the issuing of our order in council, which must come at the end of October or shortly thereafter, to achieve a final and ultimate resolution of the various issues. What the officials are now seeking is some kind of interim arrangement that will permit Canada to proceed on or about January 1 with this 200-mile declaration and the United States, I believe, in March 1977.
In the meantime there will unquestionably be issues left unsolved. What we are seeking is an interim arrangement while discussions are proceeding toward what we hope will be a mutually satisfactory solution over time. However, the hon. member is very experienced in this matter and I think would agree with me that this is not something that is going to be settled in two or three months.

Yesterday at approximately 10 a.m. the air-sea rescue centre in Halifax received a distress call from a Dutch freighter 60 miles off the southeast coast of Newfoundland. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think some of the facts of this tragic case should be cleared up. An aircraft from the base in the maritimes was off the ground within 18 minutes of receiving the alert, and was on the scene within two hours of receiving the alert. I congratulate the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner) and the hon. member for Glengarry-Pre-scott-Russell (Mr. Ethier) for being appointed to their present positions. I look forward to seeing them display the same impartiality and competence as was displayed by our late colleague, Albanie Morin, who we all miss greatly.
I was amazed to note, when the by-election results of the two constituencies recently contested at the federal level were made known during the course of the present debate, how apologists on the government side attempted to explain the results. We in the Conservative party are magnanimous in victory. We will not sit back and take for granted last Monday's victorious results. We know that victories down the line will mean ultimate victory in 1978.
I see my good friend, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) in the chamber. I was very interested in his speech. It was what I call a traditional Liberal speech; that is to say, the idea is to try to convince people that black is white. The hon. member for Scarborough West and the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) both made rather interesting speeches, but they were in fact apologists for this government.
There are a number of myths that have been perpetrated by the Liberals and by the government with regard to not only these by-elections but the role of the Liberal party today. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had a soul-baring in Toronto in which he in effect discussed at some length and with some candour the difficulties facing Canada today. Unfortunately, I am inclined to agree with the ever-growing number of people in Canada who interpret the Prime Minister's remarks about difficulties in Canada as being confused about the difficulties of the Liberal party. This has been the case as long as I have been observing the political scene in Canada. Liberal govern-

ments from the time of Mackenzie King have tended to regard the Canadian future and well-being as "if it is okay for the Liberal party, it is okay for Canada."
It is rather unfortunate that an attempt is being made to read into the results of the by-elections some sort of apology for the government, saying that the only reason the Conservative party had any success is that there is some sort of English backlash. I cannot think of anything more foolish or foolhardy for the government than continuing that course of action. If we look at the results of the by-elections, particularly in Ottawa-Carleton, we see that the results substantiate that there was not an English backlash. In Cumberland township, for example, where the home polls of the Liberal candidate were located, out of 18 polls the Conservative candidate won no less than 10, and the Liberal 8. These facts must be put on the record to demonstrate that in the case of the by-elections last Monday, what bound the people together was not a backlash one way or another but a common bond of dislike for the government of the day.

However, if we are going to look at competence, we should look at the length of the last session of parliament, the longest in the history of confederation. The incompetence of the government was tangibly demonstrated when, even with a majority, they did not bring forward any sensible body of legislation. They could not get it through. It was their incompetence which caused that session to last as long as it did. It is something that is very important, because the Liberal party is now being universally rejected by the people of Canada.
Looking at the Speech from the Throne, it is fair to say that that document is a continuation of the soul-baring of the Prime Minister.

speechtext: A mea culpa.

My good friend, the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) says that it is a mea
October 20, 1976

culpa, if a document can be described in that way. If confession is good for the soul, this document is very timely. We had a philosophical approach to the very serious problems as the government saw them. We had an admission of the fact that the government has not dealt with those problems as they ought to have done, that they would try to mend their ways and act in accordance with the demands and requirements of the people of Canada.
After bringing forward that document, at the first opportunity for the government to bring forward a slate of bills to indicate the kind of leadership they say they are going to give they bring in a list of legislation that was referred to in the question period today as a bit of a joke. If this country is in the difficult straits that are indicated in the Speech from the Throne, why lead off the list of legislation that has to receive immediate attention by this House with a bill relating to Historic Sites and Monuments Act amendments? That is an indication of the paucity of legislation and ideas of this government. When I think of monuments, I think of something that stands still. When I think of something standing still, I think of this government. Therefore, it probably is appropriate for this government to bring in Bill C-2.
Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture spent a lot of time talking about his wonderful record. He is a modest fellow. Every time he visits my constituency he converts more and more people. Unfortunately, for him, he converts them from the Liberal party to other parties. The Minister talked about the absolute lack in the Speech from the Throne of any meaningful reference to agriculture. The Speech from the Throne is supposed to be an indication of the priorities that a government places on the legislation to be dealt with in a session. Therefore, the amendment of my colleague, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), seconded by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), really hit the nail on the head. It points out that this government, according to legislation which the Speech from the Throne declares it will bring forward, has absolutely no interest in the agricultural industry of this country.

It is timely to remember that when this advance concept was brought in by a Conservative government, it was subjected by ridicule by those who occupy the treasury benches today and their supporters. At that time such a scheme was regarded by members opposite as being unmanageable and it was criticized accordingly. Now, in 1976, we find the government grasping this legislation to its bosom and putting it forward as its sole contribution to assisting the agricultural community, and extending the principle to one or two other groups.
The Address-Mr. Hnatyshyn
The people of western Canada have reacted to the Speech from the Throne as one which does virtually nothing for the average person out there.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext:
In the west today there is great apprehension concerning the future of agriculture in Saskatchewan. The Minister of Agriculture is a great joker. He has said that things were never better for the farmer, that the farmer never had it so good, the implication being that he need do nothing for them. The fact is that serious problems are facing farmers today, particularly those in western Canada. We are all grateful for the bumper crop this year, as well as for the high grade of the yield, but situations of this type often cover up serious, long term difficulties. Crops may be better, but everyone who is familiar with western Canada and, particularly, with Saskatchewan knows that costs have been rising while prices have been falling.
The cost of farming operations has risen dramatically over the last three or four years. This is all right when you have a bumper crop. It is all right when prices are high. But the cost of machinery and pesticides continues to rise. As I say, costs have risen dramatically. Five years ago, the cost of starting a grain farm of average size was in the vicinity of $50,000 to $60,000. Today, in order to get into business something like $150,000 is needed. How many people in Canada realize that an investment of this magnitude is involved? How many appreciate the return which is necessary in order to support it? Today, people are prepared to pay up to $500 per acre for better quality land. The Minister of Agriculture would do well to consider these things when assessing the situation in the west.
I am glad to see the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) in the chamber this afternoon. He is expert at playing broken records. I am glad to see him here because we want to cut down on American humour in Canada, and when the hon. member speaks Canadian humour is supreme.
I want to give a few examples of the cost increases to which I have referred. In 1976 the cost of machinery is up by 15 per cent compared to last year, and it is expected it will rise by a further 10 per cent in the coming year. This figure is ahead of the A1B guidelines. I want to know what action the government has taken to curb increases of this kind which affect the net income of Canadian farmers. It is true that the price of fertilizer is falling, but next spring I expect it will go up again. The cost of fuel, pesticides and other supplies needed to operate a farm can amount to $50 per acre. Nevertheless, the minister does not seem to appreciate the situation. He appears unaware of the serious problems on the horizon. If his sole gesture toward the agricultural community is to be this legislation, one sentence, or at the most a short paragraph in the Speech from the Throne, this confirms my impression that he should move to some other portfolio, possibly finance or consumer affairs. It would be better for him to employ his talents

October 20, 1976
The Address-Mr. Hnatyshyn
there than being Minister of Agriculture presiding over the disintegration of a great industry.
Many people in western Canada were disappointed to find there was only one reference to transportation in the Speech from the Throne. This is a further validation of the allegation-I say "allegation", but I believe it is a fact-which we in this party have been making for a long time. It confirms, also, the allegation made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) when he handed in his resignation-that the party opposite does not care about western Canada. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) will understand this in the next election.
I do not propose to deal with the transportation issue in much detail at this point, but I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that in the course of the last election we heard the most elaborate promises on the part of leading figures in the party opposite with respect to transportation and a great new age for transportation in Canada. Indeed, they almost made me believe that at last a Liberal government really intended to do something in that area. I remember the statements made by the Prime Minister in Edmonton, as well as his speech in Cornwall, promising to put substantial amounts of money into urban transit. In Edmonton he referred to a wonderful concept of transcontinental trains. He was going to establish a new corporation. He was going to expand the existing transcontinental system. Provision would be made to allow passengers to place their cars aboard trains for transportation across Canada. The transcontinental service was to be made extremely attractive.
What do we find? The present Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), unfortunately-and I say "unfortunately" because this is a minister who comes from the west-is now presiding over the destruction of the passenger train service in our country. All of these are examples, Mr. Speaker, of the "black is white" theory that the government is following today.
I think we should hear from the minister in some detail in this regard. We have tried to draw him out in the question period and to give him every opportunity to do so. He should rise in his place in this House and tell us what legislation he has in mind. What about the promises that were made in the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications last April, for example, when the minister said quite specifically that he was going to introduce legislation in a number of areas, if not immediately, then early in the new session? When will the minister tell us what he has in mind?
As for Air Canada, I want to know when amendments to the act will be brought in and what their nature will be. What is the government going to do in the area of a national transportation policy? I also want to know about a ports policy and the promised change in the institutional framework. I want to know about how the St. Lawrence Seaway financing is going to be dealt with. So many promises have been made by the government that it is hard to keep track of them. You almost need a filing cabinet in your office to locate them.

Only the NDP could afford a computer. The government has been suffering in the public opinion polls, and I think for a very good and valid reason. I think the government's credibility is very much at stake, as my leader pointed out in a very forceful speech. I think this can be traced to any number of issues that have arisen during the course of the government's mandate in this parliament. It extends from the fiasco of the 180 degree shift by the government on the question of wage and price controls. People were amazed when the Prime Minister went across the country saying, "Zap, your wages are going to be frozen". I am sure the hon. member for Assiniboia will remember seeing, on television in Saskatchewan, people sitting on blocks of ice. We will all remember the government's turnabout.
I also think the Prime Minister made a very serious mistake regarding the difficulties of the air traffic controllers, and as a result his credibility has suffered. The Prime Minister has been going around this country trying to promote himself and his party as the party of unity. He made a cold and calculated decision to raise the issue to the national level before the Canadian people when he took national television time to deal with it.
I share the agony of this whole situation with the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal). I am a Canadian and he is a Canadian. I resent the Prime Minister trying to make political capital out of that kind of issue. I resent the Prime Minister of this country trying to suggest that he is the only person who can patriate the constitution. I suggest this kind of approach only demonstrates something that the Canadian people are beginning to understand more and more, namely, that this Prime Minister is less concerned about the issues we are going to face and about giving leadership than he is with his own personal place in history and in hanging on tp power at any cost.
I see that you are coming to your feet, Mr. Speaker, so I will conclude my remarks by saying that Canada will survive and become stronger after 1978 when the party of which I am a member becomes the governing party and brings a sense of reason to the governing of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I commence my remarks by congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. May I also thank hon. members on both sides of the House for the kind best wishes they have offered me in my new capacity.
Were I once again a private member, I could spend a good deal of time today making glowing references to the Speech from the Throne and taking a few minutes to justly attack the last speaker, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn). I can only say to him that were he to commit his speech to the form of an advertisement, my department would have to take a very serious look at it under the misleading advertising provisions of the legislation.
October 20, 1976

For a very few minutes, Mr. Speaker, I should like to talk about the work of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I have been minister for only one month, and therefore it is only proper that my remarks should be brief since my knowledge of the department is limited. However, I should like to deal with one aspect that has been frequently discussed recently in newspapers, namely, the apparent conflict, as some people view it, between the businessman and the consumer. They are wondering how my department can have the title of Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I have attempted to say that someone with some business experience and also some legal experience should not necessarily be denied this position as being completely unfit to serve the consumer. However, the point I should like to make is that this department has some 29 acts within its compass, ranging from competition, bankruptcy, packaging and labelling, textile labelling-a whole variety of areas concerning both the consumer and the business community.
What could perhaps be described as a common thread between these acts is that they deal with the marketplace and there is a genuine coincidence of needs within the department. The task of the department really is to make the marketplace as fair and as efficient as possible. It is not to act as a regulator or as a policeman but, rather, to permit growth of a vigorous and powerful free enterprise community and to see it thrive. At the same time, the department must make certain that the powerful in the marketplace cannot crush the weaker yet efficient members as well.
The emphasis of the department in past years has, it is true, been on the consumer. This has been occasioned by the fact that it is the consumer who is in the weaker position in the marketplace. The need for protection of the consumer is greater than that of the business operator. The fact is that the pendulum may have swung from "Let buyer beware", closer to "Let seller beware". Nonetheless, I suggest that the department takes an even-handed approach in general to the marketplace. I think that even the most vigorous advocate of free enterprise would not wish us to return to the day when P. T. Barnum could exult in the fact that a sucker is born every minute, to be exploited.
The role of the government in the affairs of Canadians is not a new issue but an old one. The fact is that government has played a larger and larger part in our activities, whether it be in regulating agriculture or regulating transportation and communications. There is a large place in the marketplace for government, but it is the underlying philosophy of this government that the marketplace shall not be destroyed or weakened by government but will, hopefully, be enhanced in its efforts. It is in this respect that we in the department are concerned with the introduction of the second phase of the competition bill.
Doing this, I shall only continue the work which has already been accomplished by my predecessors. Each one contributed in his way to this difficult task over the years. I want to
The Address-Mr. Abbott
mention particularly the work done by the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) who succeeded in having the first part of the competition policy adopted. Thanks to his patience, his skill, his kindness and his working capacity, he succeeded where others failed.

He demonstrated, under considerable difficulty, at the committee stage what can be done by firm but conciliatory attitudes. I hope that in the months to come as we introduce phase II of the competition policy I can do at least partially as well. The prospects in that bill have aroused considerable concern among all sectors of the economy. I have already had discussions with businessmen and with consumers. There are very difficult policy choices involved, for industry, we know, must be subjected to competition, yet many today are protected by tariff walls, and it is the job, in devising a competition policy, to ensure that industry is able to thrive without damaging less powerful members of that community.
The complaints I have received from small business operators, particularly in the small retailing field, concern the inability of these retailers to purchase in the same advantageous manner in which the large giants of the industry may do. It serves to illustrate my point when I say that here is an example of the difficult choices we have to make in devising the act. We do not wish to eliminate the real efficiencies and advantages conferred by size in purchasing, yet we must deal with the question of how the small retailer or a collection of small retailers may take advantage of volume purchasing.
Therefore, I think that in the next few months this is going to be an important bill which parliament may deal with, and I hope I can serve to persuade my colleagues on all sides of the House of the benefits of this legislation and that it is passed without further delay. It has been a long time arriving.

The people are reacting very positively so far, and I am sure when they see the bill they will react even more positively.
In addition to the competition bill, I hope at a very early stage to introduce legislation dealing with consumer credit. As all members are aware, there has been tremendous growth in this form of borrowing. It is important that in Canada today we have uniform legislation and that we give adequate protection to the borrower to ensure that he or she receives all the information required to make a responsible decision in this area. Therefore, I hope, again, that this legislation will be viewed not as restrictive to those borrowing in the business community, for that is not its intention, and that it will not simply be regarded as a bill designed only to help the consumer, but will be recognized as a valuable piece of legislation that will help the whole marketplace and, of course, the individual consumer.
In addition to this measure, I am hopeful that we will bring in some long overdue legislation which died on the last order paper, concerning bankruptcy and insolvency. Hon. members

October 20, 1976
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
are aware that we are doing studies on the question of trademarks, and perhaps before the end of the session we will be introducing legislation in this area as well.
As I indicated, Mr. Speaker, I do not feel that my term in office would justify a lengthy speech and I know you will be relieved to learn that. However, I do want to complete my remarks by dealing with a subject which I think is close to all of us, and that is the question of national unity.
All members on both sides must ask themselves occasionally what accidents of fate brought us together in this place, and for what purpose. So many frustrations, absences from home, demands on time and energy and criticism at every turn surely make this a valid question. For most of us it is a privilege superior to any other that may be extended to a Canadian. But as Canadians drawn from every point of this country, we surely have an obligation not only to make the parliamentary system work but also to convince Canadians from all provinces that Canada is a country worth preserving. It seems almost beyond belief that citizens in a country so uniquely blessed should question whether it is worth preserving as a nation. Surely there are few, if any, members here who do not believe there must be a supreme effort made to preserve our national unity. This is the fundamental issue which lies at the basis of this country's national existence.
Speaking as a Liberal partisan, in what is, I hope, the better sense of the term, I do not support this party and this government because it is always right. I do not support the Liberal government because I have always been in agreement with every policy. I can even look across the floor and see members who would do a very good job as ministers in any government. The real reason I support the Liberal government is that it has at the core of its justification for existence the determination to maintain the unity of this country.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have the opportunity today to follow the new Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott). As the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) said, he knows him better than I do and he knew his father. I know the minister will smile at this, but some years ago when I was vice-president of the junior chamber of commerce of Canada, I travelled with Mr. Abbott Sr. and got to know him pretty well. I should like to relate this one incident as I think it will start off my address in the proper atmosphere.

We were driving from Saskatoon to a place called Tisdale. This was in the forties. The federal government, which was then Liberal, had just called an election following a budget in which it had taken the tax off soft drinks. It was a hot day and we stopped in a little village to buy soft drinks. Gordon Blair, who was a member of this House, was with us. We asked for soft drinks, and the young lad at the counter said they would not cost as much that day because Mr. Abbott had taken the tax off. Gordon Blair said that Mr. Abbott was with us in the car. Looking at Mr. Abbott Sr., the young lad said, "If he is Abbott, I am Mackenzie King". He did not realize that he was really looking at Mr. Abbott.
The minister, in his remarks, referred to unity. I am certain that the Liberal party has made a contribution to unity and I am confident that every member of this House of Commons since confederation has basically stood for unity. In fact, the Progressive Conservative party was the party of confederation that brought this country together.
When I hear a line like that, saying that they have some monopoly on unity, I wonder whether there is something wrong at the present time in their own caucus. Perhaps they are bothered not only by the fact that there is disunity in the caucus but also by a feeling that they are perhaps bringing about some disunity across this country. Having said that, I wish to address myself and the House to some of the vital legal concerns of the Canadian people as to the trend being followed by this government, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and by others influencing him in reference to the administration of justice.
Before doing so, I wish to incorporate all the congratulatory words used in this debate by others with regard to both the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. Both hon. members, namely, the one from Restigouche and the one from Lafontaine-Rosemont, did credit to themselves and this chamber, and tried to do credit to the government in their very thoughtful and able addresses. Congratulations to both hon. members.
Now I wish to deal with three subjects. The first concerns a bill that was introduced and then dropped from the order paper. Both the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General presented jointly or in partnership last session a bill, namely, Bill C-83, which died on the order paper because the Liberals let it die. It was entitled "An act for the better protection of Canadian society against perpetrators of violent and other crime". It contained amendments and, therefore, changes to the Criminal Code in five fields.
I wish to emphasize that. It did not investigate gun control alone. It legislated also in respect of dangerous offenders who under the Criminal Code are still called habitual criminals. It contained wiretapping legislation to abolish the 90-day notice necessary to be given to the subject after a judge has given authorization to wiretap the subject's telephone. Then it allegedly gave the provinces jurisdiction to conduct special crime inquiries in reference to crime going on within that
October 20, 1976

particular province's borders, on which the Supreme Court of Canada ruled and in respect of which they now have jurisdiction. Then there were the changes in the parole procedure.
So although this bill is referred as the gun control bill, it dealt with five phrases of amendments to the Criminal Code. The government called this legal criminal conglomeration of amendments "the peace and security package". Later it became erroneously known as the gun bill. This is only part of the story. This bill contained 73 pages, 39 pages of which dealt with the use, the storage, the licensing of guns and ammunition. The remainder of the bill dealt with the other four matters I mentioned.
In particular, that portion of the bill dealing with wiretapping gunned down the right to privacy and to civil rights enjoyed by all Canadians during the lifetime of this nation. The Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs sat 75 hours, held 38 meetings and heard briefs from many national organizations. I might say at the outset that the bill was a bad bill. Even the government member on the committee recognized the flaws in the bill. Finally, the government brought in 54 amendments. Perhaps one or two of them might have been ours. These amendments were approved, but basically, and tragically, the bad features of the bill still remain.
I shall direct my words to that part of the bill which cannot be accepted, condoned or approved. On second reading we moved a motion that the bill be separated so that the gun control amendments could be considered apart from the other four amendments to the Criminal Code. The government refused to accept that motion. The minister spoke against the amendment and the Minister of Justice voted against the amendment, as did all government members.
The minister was trying to ram this multi-conglomeration through parliament, hoping that the people would see the little bit of good that was to be done and overlook a devil of a lot of bad. Apart from the many bad features contained in definitions and other technical parts of the gun control legislation, the government designed a new form of procedure to legislate criminal law, not by parliament but by order in council. This is unacceptable. The legislation of criminal law must be precise. It must be concise and free from ambiguity and, above all, it must be known to people as legislated by parliament, rather than made in a secret chamber by a known or unknown body, such as the federal cabinet.
I listened to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) who referred to the late Mackenzie King. When there is an attempt to deal with legislation by order in council, this is what one of the fathers of that party said in this chamber:
Now let us come to another point which I wish particularly to stress, I refer to the right set out in Magna Carta that no man shall be dispossessed of his rights without the lawful judgment of his peers under the law of the land; not the law as made by the governor in council, not the law as made by some unnamed and as yet unexisting body, but the law of the land as known to everyone. It is an essential principle of liberty and freedom that the law of the land should be known, that it should be so known that every man as he runs may read. The law should not be something which is to make its appearance in the Canada Gazette
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
after some board or governor in council, not parliament, has passed a regulation; it is something that should appear in the statutes of the country.
At the time of the committee hearings, the members of the Progressive Conservative party knew that the government members were going to try to ram through the bill, and the only amendment I could make which was acceptable to the committee and the minister was that these numerous orders in council must be referred to parliament for discussion and debate in this House. But that does not stop the cabinet going ahead now, and it does not stop this or any other cabinet in the future legislating criminal law without the approval of parliament. It does not prevent the cabinet making orders in council as they see fit, or even object to the same. The minister, the government, and some members of the media appear to have failed to appreciate the inherent dangers in such a practice when it affects one's civil rights and liberties in this country.
Let me turn to another feature of Bill C-83. This deals with wiretapping. I am glad to see the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) in the House, because I know he will agree with what I say. I know his views. I know he believes in the perpetuation of civil rights. We find totally unacceptable the fact that the government would call for the abolition of the 90-day notice which must be given to a subject whose telephone is being wiretapped by the police, as authorized by a judge, so that the person may be made aware that his or her private rights have been interfered with. I shall not quote the section of the Criminal Code to which I refer. It is section 178.23(1), which states that the Attorney General of a province or the Solicitor General of Canada shall give notification within 90 days which, if necessary, can be extended by a judge if the investigation involves syndicated crime.
The concerned committee members of the opposition managed to move an amendment to this abolition of notice so that the extention or the abridging of time must not go on indefinitely. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) and myself took a very dim view of the subject I am now discussing. The government would not accept anything short of a maximum five-year period. I am totally dissatisfied with this procedure. It is very interesting to note that 556 wiretapping permissions were granted in 1976, that only one was refused and that there were two cases of refused extensions. There were only two cases where extention of time was refused.
I am concerned about solicitor-client conversations being bugged, because communications between a barrister or solicitor and his client are privileged and must be that way if the liberty and freedom of the subject is to be safeguarded. A case in my own city was brought to my attention by a trial lawyer. That case is now before the courts. In that case a conversation between the trial lawyer and his client was bugged. The Crown was able to determine the defence, and the privilege of communication between the solicitor and his client was usurped. I am therefore concerned about the bugging of professional people's private communications.

October 20, 1976
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
I am concerned about private industrial communications being bugged. For example, with regard to exploration and development in the oil industry there is a necessity for secrecy. That is also true in the manufacturing and patent industries. I am concerned about the private communications of public servants being bugged. I am concerned about ail private conversations being bugged unless proper authorization has been granted in accordance with the terms and conditions of the Criminal Code.
A time period longer than 90 days simply increases the wiretap powers of the police and removes essential safeguards from citizens. This 90-day notice serves as a safeguard against excessive bugging. The government does not need to extend the 90-day notice because at present the courts have full power to do it anyhow. If notification is repealed altogether, how would section 178.21 have any effectiveness? This provision allows courts to award punitive damages when convicting accused people for unlawful interception. If this were ever to be the case, proper authorities could illegally intercept private communications and the supposed victim would not be aware that he was being observed, because the observation itself would be concealed. The only reason the lawyer to whom I referred knew his telephone was bugged when he was talking to his client was that his client received a notice; otherwise he would not have known. A victim cannot assess the legality of surveillance unless he is notified. Surely he is entitled to that privilege. Only then can the criminal process be initiated.
As I understand the Criminal Code, derivative evidence- and that means evidence which is derived from this source- obtained from illegal wiretapping would be a crime in itself and not admissible under the code. Under the bill the government is trying to bring in, that illegal bugging, although an offence under the Code, would be made admissible against people. That, of course, is contrary to what I understand to be the common law of this country and the civil rights of Canadians. We find legislation suggested in this form unacceptable. When persons here and in the media describe it as gun legislation, they have not read the bill. The nickname is partly correct, though, because the legislation would gun down Canadian civil rights. It would be contrary to the common law and to the Bill of Rights of this country.
Let me deal with another question. At the moment my greatest concern, and the greatest concern of all trial lawyers and those who understand the question of civil liberties, has to do with the recommendation of certain people that we abolish preliminary hearings in criminal cases and abolish the jury system for certain kinds of indictable offences. This week I asked the minister a question in this House and he responded as follows:
I made a speech in Vancouver in which I said that we do not intend to interfere with the jury system, the right of the accused to remain silent, and the protection against self-incrimination . . . but I am not in a position to say at this time whether any bill will be introduced relating to that matter.
What kind of bill is he going to bring in? One on plain white paper? If he is not going to do the things he has been talking about, for what reason does he need a bill? The other day I asked him to come clean; that is why he has been nicknamed

Mr. Clean. I asked him to give answers and not to pussyfoot around. I told him we wanted to know because in the committee we were faced with that monstrosity, Bill C-83, and we may be faced with another monstrosity. It seems to me that this government and this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who before becoming leader of the Liberal party and Prime Minister had the image of a man standing for civil rights are bent on destroying civil liberties as we understand them in the common law of this country.

speechtext:
The minister said that he was not in a position to say whether the bill will be introduced. The suggestion to reduce the number of jury trials and abolish preliminary hearings for the purpose of expediting trials is not the answer and has been rejected by the leaders of the criminal section of the Canadian Bar Association.
In accordance with the recommendations of the Law Reform Commission, we should set up family courts to take out of the jurisdiction of superior courts in the various provinces such matters as divorce and property settlement. That would expedite trials because it would get rid of trial dockets in many centres. Much of the time of superior courts is taken up with divorce work, property settlements and matrimonial affairs. In large urban areas like Toronto or Vancouver we should increase the number of judges to take care of the backlog of cases. These two suggestions would solve the problem without interfering with the private and civil rights of Canadians.
The proposal to eliminate trials by jury, and preliminary hearings, is based on a working paper which I understand was prepared by officials of the Department of Justice. That is rather shocking to me. It is also based on a Law Reform Commission study of pre-trial procedures. The Minister of Justice states that the paper is based on a system of complete Crown disclosure before trial, by which prosecutors would be obliged to disclose, by way of a pre-trial hearing, all of the case against the accused. Through this recommendation it is hoped that many pre-trial and trial delays can be eliminated. However, that is really the very purpose of preliminary hearings. A preliminary hearing is a vehicle by which defence counsel can determine the case against a person. Then when he gets before a judge and jury he can present his case properly. If there are to be any changes leading to fewer preliminary hearings, they should be made with reference to very unimpor-
October 20, 1976

tant charges. I am against any changes with regard to charges which could result in long-term imprisonment.
I seriously question whether one can eliminate the delay and backlog in the system by implementing these new recommendations without affecting the fundamental rights of accused persons. The defence uses the preliminary hearing as a vehicle to find out what the Crown has against the accused and to help in preparing the defence. To eliminate the preliminary hearing would be to revert to the system where a person is guilty until proved innocent. If there are to be any major changes in preliminary hearing procedures or in trial by jury procedures, I want the Minister of Justice to restate the promises he made to the Vancouver judges. I think I should put on the record what he said, because we cannot drag it out of him in the House. He said the following:
But let there be three things made very clear. Firstly, that any changes should not tamper with the jury system.
Thank you, Mr. Minister of Justice.
I need no lectures on the importance of jury trials ... Secondly, I firmly believe that we should not change the basic principles of presumption of innocence and the Crown's onus of proof. Thirdly, I agree that we should not remove the right of the accused to remain silent.
The choosing of 12 ordinary persons to form a jury represents a safeguard and a buffer and is one of the most fundamental parts of our freedom. I wish to quote a Toronto lawyer, the ombudsman of Ontario and a friend of mine, Arthur Maloney, as follows:
Of all the institutions contrived by imperfect man for his own safety and security the jury stands out like a beacon whose glare, far from diminishing, has become more dazzling over the long centuries of its history.
I might add to that, over the long centuries of our judicial history. By even courting proposals such as the reduction in the number of preliminary hearings and jury trials, the Minister of Justice is plunging too far, too fast and too dangerously. The right to be tried by a jury of our peers is as old as Magna Carta. That was one of its terms, and must not lightly be put aside. The right of an accused to remain silent is a fundamental right. One would think that in 1976 it would not be necessary to mention that. The Globe arid Mail supported me in that. I do not always have Geoff Stevens of the Globe and Mail behind me.
We must stand on guard at all times, Mr. Speaker. There has been some suggestion that the Crown would be able to examine the accused on evidence that the Crown, in its opinion, could substantiate. One of the old cases which re-establishes this rule and which the Supreme Court of Canada supports is Ibraham v. The King, (1914) Appeal Cases, 599, a judgment of Lord Lumner which is supported by Canadian courts. At page 609 he said:
It has long been established as a positive rule of English criminal law, that no statement by an accused is admissible in evidence against him unless it is shown by the prosecution to have been a voluntary statement, in the sense that it has not been obtained from him either by fear of prejudice or hope of advantage exercised or held out by a person in authority.
The Address-Mr. Woolliams
These rules only apply, of course, when statements are made and given by the accused to people in authority. But a new practice is growing up whereby those in authority-and this is more dangerous than ever-the police, the Crown, arbitrarily place the accused person in a mental hospital for the purpose of observation and treatment by either a psychiatrist or psychologist and obtain by_ this method a statement which the police would not be allowed to admit in evidence. These are medical people and not people in authority and an accused will often place confidence in doctors.
I have cases right now where there is some question of the mental stability or mental capacity of the accused. A person was placed in a medical hospital, and not only was he interrogated by the psychiatrist, to whom he gave his whole confidence but, as I was told by the Crown's psychiatrist, he had a blackout. The psychiatrist told me that when you have a blackout and are questioned by a psychiatrist or a psychologist, you try to fill the vacuum. Suppose the person being questioned by a psychiatrist or a psychologist fills the vacuum and says, "I might have done it; I could have done it; I do not know." What effect might that have upon a jury? Mr. Speaker, the police cannot get evidence in like that, so why should it be brought through the back door by medical people hired by the Crown, with the accused ordered to be there by the judge? I say this is very dangerous, Mr. Speaker, and, of course, it is not only dangerous but the law is not very definite on it.
There are many cases, Mr. Speaker, and one which concerns me is an old one which I think was mentioned in the Vallain-court case this year in the Supreme Court of Canada. It is Regina v. Roadhouse (1934) 61 Criminal Cases of Canada, 191. Last, but not least, is the Vallaincourt case (1976) 1 Supreme Court Reports, 13. A very distinguished Montrealer, Professor Kaufman, in his book "Admissibility of Confessions" had this to say:
These statements are suggestive of guilt and the point of law is raised that this evidence was inadmissible because the accused, being in custody and handed over temporarily for treatment while police officers remained in close attendance (without, however, so far as the evidence shows, hearing the statements) the doctor must in law be regarded as a person in authority.
But the court disagreed and said:
Ordinarily a person in authority is one engaged in the "arrest, detention, examination, or prosecution" of the accused... Dr. Shaw stood in the same position as the wife of an arresting officer if the accused had been taken to his home for first-aid treatment at her hands, administered under the circumstances disclosed in this case. The doctor was not deputized by the police to act on their behalf nor was he performing any function-
The Statement made to the doctors was therefore admitted as evidence. I say this is a dangerous process, Mr. Speaker. If in this speech I have left any impression at all, I hope it is that the liberty and freedom of the subject is all-important. I think this House knows where I stand on crime. Certainly, those who commit-

speechtext: You are against it.

speechtext:
I am certainly against the wrong kind of evidence. It is better to let one guilty person go free than to

October 20, 1976
The Address-Mr. Nystrom
hang ten innocent people or send them to jail. I say the Minister of Justice should look at this matter.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I am one of those who believes that the only evidence that should be admitted is on the test of truth. When a person is induced, or falsely or fraudulently encouraged by psychiatrists or psychologists to try to fill the vacuum of things they do not know are the complete truth, that should be disregarded as evidence.
In the matters that I have mentioned today, if the steps that this government seems to be taking are to be the funeral of liberty and freedom and the end of the fundamental right to be tried by a jury of our peers, then I would not think this Minister of Justice would even want to be an honorary pallbearer at that funeral.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I want to say a few words on the subject of food and agriculture. I see the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goo-dale) sitting by, anxiously waiting to pick up some valuable information to take back to his constituents.
I wish to introduce something a little different this afternoon. I want to speak about what I think is going to be a real problem, not only today but in the future, in the area of food and agriculture. I, for one, believe that by the end of this century we will have a real crisis in the shortage of food and protein in the world community. All we have to do is look at some of the population statistics. The world's population is about four billion, and we are unable to feed them all. Some say that about 16,000 people die of starvation every day, while thousands of others die of diseases connected with some form of malnutrition.
If present trends continue, the world's population will probably double by the year 2000. If we cannot feed the people now, how will we do it a few years ahead unless the programs of this and other governments change radically? I think we must realize, however, that this country obviously cannot feed the hungry of the world. We would be misleading ourselves to think we could be the food basket of the world community. I think we do have a role to play, however, in helping to feed other people by maximizing food production in this country. Our prime object as a nation, however, must be to help other countries to become self-reliant, to be able to feed themselves. We must provide the proper technology and know-how to enable them to produce their own food in quantities sufficient to feed their own people.
We not only have to be concerned about the problem of food in the world, but about the problem of food in our own country. Many people think that we have no food problem in Canada because we produce efficiently and no one goes hungry. But it is not quite that simple, Mr. Speaker. A study produced by the Food Prices Review Board about a year ago pointed out that about 70 per cent of old age pensioners in Canada suffered from a lack of calcium in their diet. Yet we recently had a surplus of various milk products. Before it folded, that same board said that about 40 per cent of the
[Mr. WoolIiams.J
hospital days in Canada could possibly be linked to bad nutrition.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And alcohol.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Alcohol too. Think of the junk foods- children in school drinking Cokes and Pepsis, eating hot dogs, hamburgers, chips, candies, chocolate bars and all kinds of really junky foods. I am glad the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mrs. Campagnolo) is here, because I know she is concerned about this. If we had sensible policies and proper programs we could get rid of the Coke machines and other things in the schools and provide milk and fresh fruit and vegetables instead.
If the Food Prices Review Board is right in saying that about 40 per cent of hospital days are connected with malnutrition, just think how we could bring down the cost of medicare and hospital accommodation through a good program of nutrition. Many diseases and health problems could be prevented. We will not have good policies in this country, however, unless we devise a comprehensive food and agricultural program, one that is integrated and takes into account the interests of the producer and the consumer. We need a farm program which will guarantee farmers a decent income and make sure they are able to stay on the land. At the same time, we need a program which will encourage the production of food for the consumer at the lowest possible cost, so that all the people of Canada can afford to buy good food at reasonable prices.
Ahead of us I see many serious difficulties. I see a crisis facing this country in the future. I see, as does the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), the threat which large, powerful corporations in the agricultural field pose to the way of life of farmers and the existence of orderly marketing, farm organizations and individual farms. I see a crisis ahead to do with the use of our farm land.
Let us consider our land. We are one of the few countries of the world able to produce a massive surplus of food if we put our minds to it. If we grow all the food we can, we shall contribute to the well-being of the world's peoples, fortify our rural economy, allow farmers to prosper and set this country on its feet economically, because the end result of this process would be full employment. Mr. Speaker, we have one half of 1 per cent of the world population, and 3 per cent of the world's arable, food-producing land. What is to happen to that land? There is little control over the land in most of Canada. Every day much of our good land goes out of production. Just look at the statistics if you want to see what is happening. They are terrifying.
This country's urban centres cover 0.4 per cent of the nation's land surface; and remember most of our land cannot be used for farming. Only about 4 per cent of it is suitable for farming. Most of our urban centres, our cities, suburbs and factories, highways and hydro lines are built on this country's prime farmland. Most of the urban expansion in Canada
October 20, 1976

gobbles up good, arable farmland. If this country's urban population doubles, the amount of good, available farmland will be reduced by one-third. I repeat, if the urban population of Canada doubles, and it will double in not many years, and if we do nothing to preserve our farmland, our available farmland will be reduced by one-third. When that happens, we shall run into serious difficulties.
The Agrologist magazine said a short time ago that, given our present eating habits and technology, we could feed up to 50 million people in this country. On the other hand, if we begin to reduce the quantity of available arable land, it will not be long before we may not produce enough to feed ourselves and we shall need to import some food.
As I said, only 4 per cent of our land surface can be used for farming. That is to say, 164.15 million acres of land can be used for farming. At present we farm 107.8 million acres. In most cases only the prime agricultural land is in use. Marginal, less productive land, is not generally in use because it is more costly and less economic to farm. Every time this country's population rises by 1,000, the extra 1,000 people consume, for houses, schools, highways, and so on, between 360 acres and 1,700 acres. When you extend our urban regions, good farmland disappears. That lost farmland will not produce food in future. Therefore, why do we continue this process? Land does not grow on trees, Mr. Speaker; once it is paved over, it will not grow food.
I ask, why is this happening? The reason is that these matters are determined by the workings of the so-called free market. Around the major cities in almost every part of this country developers exercise absolute control over how they will dispose of land. Little has been done in this country to protect our farmland, to make sure it is used only for farming and not for the expansion of cities, highways and factories. These, where possible, must not be built on prime farmland. Mr. Speaker, 96 per cent of this country's land surface cannot be used for farming.
The present situation has arisen because of the federal government's abysmal record in leadership. It has done nothing to preserve farmland and has not brought forward an adequate farm policy which could serve this nation in future. So far as I know, only two provinces have acted to preserve farmland. One is my native Saskatchewan, which introduced a land banking program which is working well; the other is British Columbia-

-which has legislated the preservation of farmland for farm use only. The attitude of the other provinces with Liberal and Conservative governments and politicians has been that governments, provinces and municipalities should not interfere with the free enterprise system. They think that this country's future should be left in the hands of developers and speculators. That is not good enough, Mr. Speaker, if we want to grow enough food for our own people and help other people in the world. We must face the question squarely. I do not see how any Liberal can argue that the federal government
The Address-Mr. Nystrom
has shown leadership in this area. The question is most serious and will become even more serious within 20 or 25 years unless we act.
If we are to grow enough food in future, we must make sure that farmers remain on the land and earn a stable income. I heard the suggestion not long ago that our farmers are prosperous now that grain prices are high. Mr. Speaker, such prices are not stable. Prices for the grain producer were high, but the price has recently fallen by $1.04 per bushel. Prices are lower than they were three months ago. The price of other farm commodities is also falling. Also, we all know of the difficulties of the cow-calf producer. Many of them are going bankrupt. Many mixed farmers face hard times.
You see, in my constituency and the constituency of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, a great deal of rural poverty. Some farmers in my riding do not have in their homes water and sewer facilities and the other modern amenities which we in this House take for granted. The same can be said of farmers all across this country-in Quebec, New Brunswick and other areas. Their story is the same.
I bring these problems forward to show that our stabilization legislation is not the only answer If it were, farmers would not be forced to leave the land. Too many decisions affecting the land are made by big concerns. In the process, the small producer is forgotten. Companies like Cargill, about which the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre spoke, are moving into this country and exercising ever more control over the food industry and food prices. The dominance of such companies poses a threat to our Canadian way of life. Do we want control of this major industry, agriculture, concentrated in fewer and fewer hands, or do we want to maintain our present way of life? Do we want to maintain what most farmers favour, a system of orderly marketing, wheat pools, co-operatives and marketing boards which give the farmer some clout in the marketplace?
Let us examine some of our other difficulties. Some time ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), who is responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, put feed grains on the open market. By so doing he took away some of the foundation for stable farm income. He allowed feed grains to be traded on the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, thereby giving the exchange with which the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) is connected influence over the price the farmer was to receive for that product. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre documented how large, multinational corporations involved in the grain business are moving into this country's prairie provinces. He told the House what would happen if they build huge inland terminals. I ask, where does the Conservative party stand with respect to these large inland terminals being either constructed or proposed on the prairie provinces? The effect of these terminals will be this: smaller elevators all over the prairies will be closed and more and more power and wealth will be concentrated in the hands of huge corporations.

October 20,1976
The Address-Mr. Nystrom
What is going to happen to rural society with the abandonment of rail lines? What is going to happen to the consumer if nothing is done about the immense power of some of the processors, retailers and wholesalers in this country? What will happen as corporations get larger and have more say about the price people pay for food? I need only refer to the last report of the Food Prices Review Board which pointed out that there are four large retailers in this country, Weston-Loblaws, Safeway, Dominion stores and Steinbergs. They control a very large proportion of the retail food markets in Canada. In places such as the prairies, between 80 and 90 per cent of the market is controlled by three or four of these large corporations. Is there any competition when these large corporate giants get together? I suggest there is not.
If the large corporations such as Cargill Grain, Continental Grain and a number of others south of the border continue to move into the producing sector, what will happen to the price of food in this country? Food is too important to be left to the private sector. Food is the right of all Canadians. The price of food should be controlled by those who produce food and by the people who consume it.
More assistance should be given to the farmers, particularly those with small farms and those who want to begin farming. There should be marketing boards for farm commodities, so that the producers can have some clout in the marketplace with regard to the remuneration they receive. One need only look at one area to see what I mean. I refer to the cow-calf producer. Recently, in my constituency, I talked to farmers who had sold young calves in the marketplace for as low as $20 and $30. What happens at the retail and when a person is buying this beef a Weston-Loblaws, Safeway or a Steinberg store here in Ottawa? That drop in price which the producer is suffering is not being reflected at the retail end when someone is purchasing it.
It is a real crime for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to get up in this House time and again and give us the same old baloney about agriculture and how difficult it is to do anything for the cow-calf producer, even though he has not produced any program for them. The provinces had to act unilaterally to provide assistance for cow-calf producers. Alberta put $40 million into a plan. Saskatchewan put $32 million into a plan in order to stop cow-calf producers going out of production. However, the Minister of Agriculture refuses to put any money into a plan to try and help cow-calf producers. It is not just the cow-calf producer who will suffer. It is not just the fact that the small farmer will be put out of business. In the long run, it will be the consumer who will suffer.
Farmers will sell their cows more and more rapidly as the price of beef to the producer drops. In a few years there will be a shortage of beef in this country. Prices will skyrocket as the retailers and wholesalers have a virtual monopoly. The consumer will be ripped-off, having to pay very high prices. The government will then have a real problem. If cattle and beef are left on the open market and the price of these commodities
[Mr. Nystrom.)
is controlled by speculators, huge corporations, packing houses and retail companies, there will be a real problem. What we need at this time is a national beef marketing agency or board that will stabilize the price of beef in this country. The Minister of Agriculture says he is in favour of that. I would like to see him give some leadership in promoting this idea.
The minister should hold a plebiscite to determine whether cattle producers in this country want a marketing agency. If such a plebiscite were held, I believe the vote would be a resounding "yes." The hon. member for Assiniboia may have some large ranches in his constituency. However, if hd visits my constituency he will Find that the overwhelming majority of farmers want a beef marketing agency. I need only refer to a meeting that took place in northwestern Saskatchewan a few days ago. The group of farmers who gathered there ^ngrily demanded a national marketing board for beef. Organizations are being formed in my constituency by ordinary farmers, not the huge cattle ranchers. They do not believe the Canadian Cattlemen's Association speaks for them. They want a national marketing agency. They want some protection in the marketplace. Why should the price of their labour be determined by Canada Packers, Burns, the huge retail stores in this country, or speculators in the United States? Why not a marketing board for beef so that the farmers have some clout and some say about what they will get for their commodity? The farmers should get some benefit for their labour.
I sometimes become rather annoyed with the Canadian Cattlemen's Association and their political organs such as the hon. member for Assiniboia, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt and some of the Tories who a few years ago said they did not want any government involvement or interference, that they were free enterprises in a free market. Now the price of cattle is falling and these same people in the Cattlemen's Association want some support. They say they are suffering in the so-called free enterprise economy which they fought so hard to preserve. Support should be given to the small beef farmer now. At the same time, we should ensure that he has a marketing agency or board when times are good as well as when they are bad. Let us have some consistency in the cattle policy of this country.
There is something else I want to mention before my time runs out. A very important issue will soon be debated on the prairies. A few years ago the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board took domestic feed grains out of the purview of the Wheat Board. He promised the western farmers a plebiscite on feed grains being taken out of the Wheat Board. Recently he announced that a plebiscite would be held. It may be late, but he says it will be held. We do not know what question will be asked, or who will have the right to vote. We want the minister to give the prairie farmers a chance to have all grains produced on the prairies under the purview of the Canadian Wheat Board.
There will be a real Fight on the prairies. Huge businesses, the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, the Liberal party and many of the Conservative party will support keeping feed grains on the open market. There is going to be a fight. It is going to be one
October 20, 1976

of the biggest fights we have seen on the prairies. I should like to quote from the Globe and Mail. On October 15, the Globe and Mail carried an article entitled "Grain marketing plebiscite called crucial test confronting farmers". I quote:
A forthcoming plebiscite on Canada's grain marketing system is shaping up as one of the most crucial tests ever to confront the private grain industry, according to R. S. Ennis, president of the Winnipeg Commodities Exchange.
The president of the Winnipeg Commodities Exchange made it clear he was attempting to influence farmers to vote for a continuing role for the private grain industry. "In the coming year it will be necessary for each one of us to make the benefits of free marketing known to the public.''
The Winnipeg Grain Exchange is going to be involved in this campaign. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that my party will also be involved in the campaign, but on the other side. We believe the government should know why it should place all prairie grains within the purview of the Wheat Board. If the hon. member for Assiniboia does not agree, he can debate this issue with me in my constituency any time he wishes. I am absolutely confident that the wheat pools in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, together with the UGG, the National Farmers' Union, the Federation of Agriculture, as well as the governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, would agree that all prairie grains should come under the purview of the Wheat Board.

Why should not the farmer, having produced that food, reap all the benefits along with the consumer, the latter having the advantage of a lower price at the other end? This is the important issue we are facing in the west. It is one which has been with us a number of years, one which we believe we had disposed of until the Minister of Transport began to play around with the power of the Wheat Board.
I remember my grandfather telling me stories a few years ago about the days before the Wheat Board. He told me that in the fall of the year farmers would sell their grain because they had to pay taxes, buy clothes for their children for the
The Address-Mr. J. R. Gauthier winter and meet a number of other seasonal expenses. So they would all go to the elevators to sell their grain. They didn't have any clout; there was no marketing board. The price would fall to a few cents a bushel. But in the winter months the speculators who had purchased that grain were able to sell it for much more than they had paid. Today, Mr. Speaker, we have a Wheat Board which ensures that there is a uniform price paid for wheat and we in this party want to put all grain under the purview of the board.
Thus, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin):
That the amendment be amended by inserting therein, immediately after the words "Australia and New Zealand", the following:
