speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I wish to congratulate the movers of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. We must recognize that our colleagues from Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) and Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) are excellent members devoted to their ridings. Furthermore, they have proved both in the House of Commons and in committees that they are outstanding parliamentarians.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to deal with two themes. I am personally interested in the first one, namely the situation of French-speaking minorities outside Quebec, and the second may perhaps interest more particularly those who are set on the question of "bilingualisation" or the learning of a second language, namely the problems we are now facing in Canada when it comes to learning the official languages and the important role of the federal government in this area. How far can we in the federal government go in the field of education without transgressing section 93 of the British North America Act?
Mr. Speaker, as parliamentary secretary, I had the opportunity to travel throughout the country this year. So, I met Canadians from both the east and the west. In addition to fulfilling my official duties, I tried to urge those people to give me their reactions or to tell me how we should build Canada.
As all hon. members, I had the opportunity to read erroneous quotations, in Vancouver, Edmonton, Ottawa, Halifax, Quebec City or in other places. I would like to read some of them and, surely, they will not surprise anybody. Here is the first erroneous quotation:
The federal government is shoving French down English throats.
The second erroneous quotation:
Bilingualism is a goal of the Liberal party alone.
The third erroneous quotation:
French Canadians outside Quebec are just picturesque. They mix with the English-speaking majority at a frightening rate.
The few remarks I was quoting, Mr. Speaker, were not concocted by some biased newspapermen, but actual comments from Canadians. We are certainly faced with a problem

October 20, 1976
The Address-Mr. J. R. Gauthier of a national nature. Intolerance, bigotry, even empty gibes often verge on a mild form of racism. The Larousse dictionary defines racism as follows: "A system asserting the superiority of one racial group over the others, urging in particular the segregation of the latter within a country, or even aiming at the extermination of some minority".
Evidently, many Canadians are ignorant of this country's history. More disturbing still, the majority of Canadians, both in English-speaking provinces and in Quebec, are not aware that there are outside Quebec nearly one million Canadians having French as their mother tongue.
I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to speak about this group of French-speaking Canadians who live outside Quebec and who often have to make the best of difficult situations. There are one million of them, responsible for the future of a united Canada and respectful of the rights of minorities. These people-who, unfortunately, are too often forgotten-exist and 1 am one of them. According to our ability, we can and we wish to render great services to our country, if we are allowed to do so. We have proved our perseverance and our strength while respecting others' rights. We have fought for our rights, we have overcome a law which prohibited education in our mother tongue, we have survived although we were refused education in our language subsidized by public funds; we have struggled with firmness and today, longing for better understanding, we continue to fight in our quest for legislation which is supposed to promote justice.
French-speaking Canadians are not just another ethnic group. As co-founders of this country, they are on equal terms with the English-speaking majority. Canada's identity is altogether different from that of any other country. Canada is a nation which gathers together two cultures, each of whom can, thanks to its heritage and its ancestral characteristics, work in conjunction with the other to obtain results of the highest quality. There is a third group in Canada which plays an increasingly important and active part in every aspect of Canadian life and which is of neither French nor English origin. I am of course referring to Canadians from various ethnic groups who have deliberately chosen to leave their home country to find a better life and a more promising future. Of their own initiative, these people have decided to adopt our country. According to dictionaries, the word "adopt" is defined as follows; to choose and use as one's own... to accept. That is precisely what these people did: they considered opportunities for a better future in Canada, they knew what they would find in Canada if they came over, they accepted her for what she is worth and made her their own country, that of their children and of future generations.
True, most of these new Canadians, after starting their new homes, have predominantly gravitated toward the English language; it is also true that they were not always made aware of the presence of French-speaking Canadians, nor exposed to the French language or culture. For reasons which are readily understandable, many Canadians have come to place French-
[Mr. Gauthier (Ottawa-Vanier).l
speaking Canadians with the Danes, the Ukrainians, the Germans, the Italians, the Japanese, and many more. I noted, especially in western Canada, that majority ethnic groups often refer to the following argument: Would it not be more logical and more profitable for the English-speaking majority to learn Ukrainian for instance instead of French? Such reasoning does not recognize that the federal government is the government of all Canadians; that it must look after the whole country and it must legislate according to national interest. For that reason, the central government does not meet only the needs of a particular city or area, it must answer the needs of the whole country. Nothing prevents Canadians from speaking several languages. But that is not the responsibility of the federal government. Indeed, we favour them by our multicultural policy.
However, the federal government as the government of all Canadians tries to meet national needs with its official language policy. That is where our responsibility lies and why we have an official language policy. I wish to come back to those erroneous quotations: The federal government is shoving French down English throats. No need for me to dwell on that false concept from which so many conflicts spring. The federal government does not impose French on anyone. Unless you are a federal public servant whose position requires both French and English, you do not need to learn either French or English. Some civil servants are bilingual now but the people they serve are not.
It is precisely because of the decision no longer to impose English on French Canadians that some ten years ago the government put forward its official languages policy. So there is no such thing as imposing or forcing anyone to learn a second language. Let us say simply that the immediate objective of the Official Languages Act is to make the government bilingual, not the citizens it serves.
When the Liberal government introduced the Official Languages Act in 1968, we got the support of all parties represented in the House of Commons. We may discuss the way to implement the policy but the principle of bilingualism remains unchanged. Of course, the government must continue to seek new and better formulas. Personally, I am convinced that we must absolutely turn our priorities toward the survival and expansion of French-speaking minority groups in Canada.
If, on the one hand, considerable amounts of money had to be spent to make the federal civil service bilingual, in many cases allowing unilingual positions to become bilingual, I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, of the importance for Canada to turn our national priorities toward the survival and expansion of French-speaking minority groups in Canada. However considerable, the amounts of money spent to date on federal and provincial programs were justified. On the one hand, a civil service with an English-speaking majority had to be changed to make it receptive and hospitable to French-speaking and bilingual Canadians. On the other hand, we must support the learning of the second language in schools. We must now- and time is running out-provide serious assistance to Frenchspeaking minorities outside Quebec.
October 20, 1976

Here is an erroneous quotation: "French Canadians outside Quebec are just picturesque. They mix with the English-speaking majority at a frightening rate". PQ members repeat it every day. If there no longer exists a French-speaking minority in English majority provinces in a little while, what is the purpose of spending millions of dollars to put up a bilingual service if there are no Canadians speaking French? It is therefore very important for me to emphasize services to French-speaking minorities outside Quebec so as to ensure their survival and development. French-speaking minorities outside Quebec are for the most part bilingual. Their motivation for becoming bilingual at an early age is essentially an economic one and a social reality. However, I do not think I am wrong in saying that when English-speaking unilinguals learn a second language, their motivation is essentially cultural, and consequently much weaker.
Millions of dollars have been spent in an attempt to help unilingual senior civil servants become bilingual. The figure of $300 million a year has been mentioned. Only 1 per cent of this amount is used for the promotion, survival and support of French-speaking people outside Quebec. Considerable amounts have also been spent with the help of the provinces to promote the teaching of both official languages in our schools. For nearly six years, the federal government has been contributing substantially to the education of official language minority groups and has also been supporting financially the teaching of a second language. Mr. Speaker, six years is not a long time.
We must not forget that, in the past, in the provinces inhabited by large groups of Canadians whose mother tongue is French, these groups did not have equal opportunities for education and that, consequently, until 1968, most of them, or 85 per cent, dropped out of school without finishing the tenth grade. This was not because they were more stupid or not as motivated, it was simply because they did not have access to the funds which would have allowed them to continue their education in French language private institutions or even in the English language public system of that time which was not designed to meet their needs.
Mr. Speaker, we have had French language high schools in Ontario for only six years. Since then, the number of students in Ottawa itself and throughout the province has tripled. Later on, I shall quote figures concerning the number of students enrolled. Since education is so important for any society and because of the difficulty faced throughout our history by French-speaking minorities outside Quebec, I would like to give a more recent and more encouraging picture, at least as concerns my own province, Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, I gathered recent statistics about school attendance for the French-speaking minority in Ontario and about the number of pupils in English schools who study French as a second language. In the elementary, the number of children attending French schools in Ontario is steadily decreasing. That is probably due to the declining birth rate
The Address-Mr. J. R. Gauthier and also, I am afraid, to the rate of assimilation into the English-speaking majority, which is rather worrying. In 196970 there were 90,397 French-speaking children in elementary schools; that number is down to 77,568 for the academic year 1975-76.
At the secondary level, figures are a little more encouraging, and vindicate the education policy of the province of Ontario in opening French secondary schools since 1969. That year, the French high-school population was 21,590; now in 197576, it is 31,442. Those high school graduates are naturally moving up to post secondary or university education.
At the high school level, we witness an encouraging increase in attendance at post-secondary institutions by the francophone minority. The Algonquin Community College, with
6,000	students, records a marked increase in francophone registrations for the school year 1974-75. As a matter of fact, full time students attending courses given in French now account for nearly 22 per cent of the college population.
At the university level, four institutions are providing courses in French. They are Hearst College, Universite Lau-rentienne, Ottawa University and St. Paul's University. There were 5,132 francophone students attending these institutions in the school year 1974-75, which represents 37 p. 100 of the total incriptions in these institutions. The projections for 197778 indicate 5,836 students, or 41.1 per cent.
It is encouraging, Mr. Speaker, to realize that the francophone minority in Ontario is seeking in increasingly larger number a more complete education and therefore greater competence.
As regards the number of English-speaking students registered in elementary schools, statistics show renewed interest in second language learning in Ontario. It is interesting to note that 569,756 students or 39.1 per cent of the school enrolment took French courses as a second language in 1971 and that progressively that number rose to 651,669 in 1975; in other words, 46.9 per cent of English-speaking students registered in English schools took French as a second language.
In high school, the situation is not so encouraging. Where 243,135 students registered for French courses in September 1971, which represented 42.3 per cent of the Ontario population, in 1975 there were only 195, 234 students or 32.3 per cent of the total secondary school enrollment. Obviously then the secondary level registered a sharp decline in second language learning.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the figures I just quoted show the seriousness of the school policy as regards French-speaking students at the secondary level in Ontario; they also show the seriousness of parents who steered their children towards elementary shools that give second language training. Yet it is alarming to realize that at the secondary level there is growing apathy towards learning a second language and that the students, because of a very permissive system, drop the second language option, be it English or French.
An important factor in the motivation for learning a second language is certainly the lack of leadership in our Canadian

The Address-Mr. J. R. Gauthier universities. In fact, in recent years Canadian universities have dropped either French or English as a prerequisite for admission to their institutions. Let us hope that Canadian universities will soon realize the merits of language training and that as a prerequisite they will demand language proficiency obtained at the secondary level.
When considering the role of the federal government in the field of minority group education, the problem is considered in relation to language policies, policies which are part of Canadian everyday life. Moreover, those language policies must be considered not only in relation to their effect on equality of learning opportunities, but also in relation to social and professional mobility, as well as to relationships between populations.
In Canada, English is the mother tongue spoken by 60 per cent of Canadians, French by 27 per cent, and a variety of other languages by 13 per cent. Moreover, French-speaking people are not limited to the province of Quebec. Indeed, French-speaking people are also found in New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Finally, in certain provinces like New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba and Prince Edward Island, there are regions where French-speaking people are the majority.
To this main linguistic division, English-French, we must add linguistic differences of people of Indian or Eskimo origin as well as differences stemming from very diversified groups who wish to maintain contact with their initial cultural background. This category is made up of about three million people. Therefore we must add multiculturalism to the official bilingualism. No need to remind the House that the Confederation was based upon an agreement between two distinct linguistic communities referred to in section 133 of the British North America Act.
Since 1969, the federal act on the implementation of both officials languages has strengthened the bilingual character of Canada. Indeed, this law stipulates that English and French are the official languages of Canada and possess and enjoy equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all the institutions of the Parliament and government of Canada. The option so selected consists in admitting that Canada is in a position to enable both languages and, consequently, both English and French culture to take part in the economic, social and political life throughout the country. To these ends, the federal government established a generous help program for the provinces to enable them to offer teaching in the minority language, and the teaching of the second language, English or French, according to the case. Federal assistance amounts to about $100 million a year.
According to Canadian practices, the provinces are responsible for the implementation of the federal programs of assistance to bilingualism. Consequently, the establishment of policies on bilingualism is made in different ways and is based on different structures. This question of assistance to bilingual teaching gives a good illustration of the difficulties and the ambiguities we notice when the federal government is prepared to give credits, and the provinces, for constitutional reasons,

want to avoid even the appearance of a communication with Ottawa.
In view of the sensitive nature of those relations, it is hard to say whether the objective of assistance to bilingualism can be achieved through education. I recognize, like many others, the merits of that hope and the willingness to achieve it. But the fact remains that the implementation of bilingualism in schools is not uniformly successful. One recognizes readily that immersion programs in kindergartens, primary and secondary schools are successful. However, one must admit that there is an insufficient number of organized courses, that there is a shortage of qualified teachers in that field. In this regard, worthy efforts are being made by granting bursaries to 5,000 teachers to enable them to get the proper training. Since 1973, efforts have been made to train teachers; those efforts should considerably improve the quality of their training for that profession.
I am of those, Mr. Speaker, who have often criticized the use the provinces made of federal funds earmarked for the official languages program. With several others, I share doubts about the use made of those funds and I recognize the constitutional limitations that restrict the federal government in its role as watch dog over the setting up of those programs and the spending of the funds.
French-speaking Canadians residing outside Quebec often deplore the lack of administrative and educational structures; they often call to our attention the powers of local school boards, seldom willing to set up French language schools or training courses in the second language; and finally, we often see a position through which the authorities want to "bilingu-alize" the institutions of these francophone Canadians, a situation which is not likely to help them keep their mother tongue nor, the way I see it, is it likely to encourage them to learn English.
It goes without saying that bilingualism is one of the most important political problems of the Canadian federation or Confederation, a problem which, in spite of the advancement achieved, can have a critical impact on the education policy. The main problem lies in that while French is considered to be the equal of English as one of the two official languages, that position remains nonetheless quite unequal.
And so it is that the French-speaking minority in Canada, whether implicitly or explicitly, requires a special kind of protection, greater than that of official equality, in order to defend itself against the risk of anglicization. Francophones, particularly those residing outside Quebec, maintain not without reason that the constitutional French-speaking element of the Canadian federation is an essential part of the creation and maintenance of separate national identities. Indeed, without the strong attachment of the French-speaking community to its language and its culture, such a national identity would have been absorbed in the greater context of English-speaking North America. That is enough to justify the need to take measures which promote a French culture in Canada with the support of the federal government, since it is the only way to create a national Canadian spirit comprising both cultures.

Expenditures earmarked for second language courses should aim mostly at preserving the French language in every part of the provinces with a high percentage of Francophones. In this regard, I readily endorse a recommendation contained in the examiners' report on the organization for Economic Corporation and Development (OECD) concerning the need to establish in Canada a national education council. In their report, published in August, 1976, the OECD examiners proposed the establishment of a national education council subsidized by the federal government and responsible for the development of French culture in Canada.
I urge hon. members to obtain a copy of a study I commissioned to Mr. Henri-Georges Belleau, of the research section of the Library of Parliament, dated October 15, 1976. I want to thank and command Mr. Belleau for his well-documented and very interesting paper. I had asked Mr. Belleau to do research on two points. First, I had asked him to summarize the OCED report on educational policies in Canada and then to examine the following question: How far can the Federal government go, as far as educational matters are concerned, without infringing the BNA Act? I would like to read into the record the conclusions of Mr. Belleau's study. I quote:
We have seen that the federal government does not deal directly or officially with educational matters. The involment of the federal government is by means of grants and transfer payments for post-secondary education; in addition, training courses are provided by the Department of Manpower and Immigration ...
Finally, as far as the training in a second language is concerned, we should aim to maintain the French language as a living language in all areas of the provinces where there is a well-established French-speaking community. Besides, the OCED investigators would recommend the creation of a national council financed by the federal government, which would promote the development of the French culture.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, if one wishes to maintain, develop and promote a Canada in which the French language will not be used extensively only in Quebec and considered elsewhere as a bit of folklore, we will have to try and support French-speaking communities outside Quebec that will show a common will to respect, promote and maintain the survival and growth of their language. If French to be used exclusively in Quebec and English in all other part of Canada, we are shifting dangerously towards a separation. What is the use of the federal governement promoting this pan-Canadian institutionalized bilingualism if in fact the bilingual services are not needed?
Mr. Speaker, I am one of those who have faith in the future and who sincerely think that we can build a country respectful and proud of its history, of its various elements and of its differences. We are not talking about a uniform Canada, we are talking about a united Canada.

The Address-Mr. Ritchie moved me to say a few words and suggest that we on this side of the House will be unable to support the subamendment. I feel it is not at all in keeping with the amendments presented by my party and, in effect, would destroy the effectiveness of our amendment, which cites the lack of co-ordination between federal and provincial authorities involving the management of our agriculture in general. In particular, it detracts from the very serious problems faced by the beef industry as a result of excessive imports of beef from Australia and New Zealand. This beef problem obviously is one of the most important questions facing farmers both in western Canada and all across the country. Indeed, it affects the farmers in Australia, New Zealand and the United States.
In his subamendment the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville cites the need to place the marketing of all prairie grains under the sole jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. Surely this is something which should be decided by the producers. I might remind my friends that the wheat pools, the UGG and the NFU do not necessarily speak completely for their rank and file. Certainly, many farmers have shown their opposition to having feed grains placed under the sole jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board.
Some time ago a plebescite was held relating to rapeseed. At that time the growers did not wish to have their grain under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. We may feel it was an incorrect decision, but it was their decision. I think we, as members of this House, must be aware of the very important fact that the growers should be the people who make the decision as to whether or not their grains should come under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. The problems of the Wheat Board are great. It is easy for the Wheat Board to sell on world markets and satisfy the growers and all segments of our country, but the problem is different when the Wheat Board must be a buyer and a seller within our country.
What about the problems we experienced in respect of feed grains in 1969 and 1970? How would they have been solved? So I suggest this is not the way in which the feed grain, rapeseed or flax situations should be solved without a plebescite of the growers.
